passage: My cousin called me greedy in front of everyone, across the tea cups at my uncle's house. I felt my face go hot. I'm Divyansh, by the way. Those are two different things, and I'm not going to let the second one burn for the first. So I took a breath, said, "I can see you're upset. passage:
Darshan asked me to come to his family's meeting about the old house in Jaipur, mostly so he would have one friendly face in the room. I sat in the corner with the tea tray.
His cousin Mahesh started loud and stayed loud. "Your side has always been greedy. Your father took the best room for thirty years." I watched Darshan's jaw tighten. He breathed out slowly and looked at the floor for a second. Then he said, "Mahesh bhai, I want a fair split, and I want all of us together at Diwali next year. Both. Let's talk about the rooms."
In the auto afterwards I asked how he had stayed so calm. He said, "I kept repeating it in my head: fair outcome, family intact. Whatever he says, those are the two things." I can't say it didn't hurt him. He was quiet all the way home.
— Noor

Friday. The night before the first meeting about Dadaji's farmland near Mysuru, Siddharth writes on the back of an envelope: "Goal: fair split. And we still eat together at Ugadi." He tucks it into his wallet.
Saturday. At the meeting his cousin Harsha says, "You city people only come back when there's something to take." The room goes still. Siddharth feels his face burn. He touches the wallet in his pocket and says, "Harsha, I can hear you're angry. I'm not here to take. I'm here to split it fairly and keep us talking." Harsha snorts, but lowers his voice.
Tuesday. Harsha messages: "Sorry about Saturday. Can we meet before the next one, just us two?" Siddharth reads it twice, then types, "Yes. Thursday?"
